title: Use One Random Constraint to Break a Creative Stalemate
subtitle: Generate a different version before judging it.
description: When familiar approaches keep producing the same result, draw or select one bounded prompt, create a reversible alternative for a few minutes, and keep only the part that improves the actual work.

lifeOsSource.hack: If you are repeating the same creative move, introduce one arbitrary but safe constraint, make a quick alternative, then judge the artifact rather than the prompt.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: Name the part of the work that feels stuck, select one prompt or constraint without hunting for the perfect one, create a separate reversible version under that constraint, stop after one useful pass, compare it with the original, and keep only the changes that improve the brief.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: What constraint did I try, what changed in the artifact, and which part—if any—is worth carrying into the real version?

faq.question: Does the random prompt decide what I should make?
faq.answer: No. The prompt only creates a temporary constraint that may reveal another direction. You still judge the result against the real goal, audience, ethics, and requirements.

faq.question: What if the prompt is irrelevant or unsafe for the brief?
faq.answer: Discard or reinterpret it. Keep the experiment reversible and do not let a creativity exercise override legal, safety, brand, accessibility, or factual constraints.

intro.html: Creative work often stalls because the same framing keeps generating the same answer. A random prompt can be useful as a temporary constraint: it forces one different pass without claiming that randomness is inherently better. The output still has to earn its place in the real artifact.

sections.title: 1. Name what is stuck
sections.html: Point to a concrete unit: the opening paragraph, layout, product flow, diagram, headline, problem angle, or another part of the work. A prompt is easier to evaluate when you know which artifact it is supposed to perturb.

sections.title: 2. Choose one bounded constraint
sections.html: Draw or select one prompt without searching for the perfect instruction. Use a generic transformation such as subtracting an element, reversing the sequence, changing the scale, making a rough visual version, or explaining the idea to a different audience. Skip any prompt that conflicts with the brief or safety boundaries.

sections.title: 3. Make a reversible variant
sections.html: Work in a copy, branch, sketch, or scratch area. Follow the constraint long enough to produce a visibly different version, but do not confuse obedience to the prompt with quality. The exercise has succeeded when it gives you something concrete to compare.

sections.title: 4. Keep only what improves the work
sections.html: Compare the variant with the original against the actual brief. Keep a stronger structure, clearer contrast, useful omission, or other specific improvement. Discard the rest without trying to justify the prompt after the fact.

editorialCuration.reason: Replace fabricated internal pilots, completion-rate and idea-count effects, pseudo-optimal deck sizes and timers, and overclaimed creativity mechanisms with a simple reversible prompt-constraint exercise.
